Kyoka.note: Comic tanka uses the traditional 5–7–5–7–7 Japanese sound-unit pattern. English syllable counting is an adaptation.

edges.evidence: The Japanese comic form uses the five-part sound-unit pattern shown under the Japanese tanka setting. English tanka can use different syllable counts and lineation.

Katauta.note: The source gives 5–7–7 and describes the question as frequent. An answer belongs to a possible larger exchange.

edges.evidence: Katauta is a constituent of sedoka; the sedoka row specifies two.

Sedoka.note: The two 5–7–7 units give six phrases. Question and answer are frequent roles rather than obligatory speech acts.

edges.evidence: The two 5–7–7 units are explicitly called katauta.

Somonka.note: The catalog identifies two voices' tanka. Each has upper and lower phrases; the second replies to the first.

edges.evidence: Declaration and reply each take the form of a tanka.

Choka.note: Alternating five- and seven-unit phrases lead into a 5–7–7 close. The catalog also allows a following tanka envoi.

edges.evidence: The catalog names tanka as an optional envoi.

Dodoitsu.note: The customary line groups count 7–7–7–5 Japanese sound units, 26 altogether. A refrain can accompany the verse in singing. English syllable counts are adaptations.

Gogyohka.note: Five line breaks normally follow phrases or breaths. Rare four- and six-line versions are documented. No fixed syllable count governs a line.

edges.evidence: The standard five-line shape is a quintain. The practice explicitly admits rare four- or six-line exceptions.

Renga / renku.note: Linked verse includes several layouts. Renku uses links and shifts; the 36-verse kasen shown here is one layout. Its two folios have four sides of 6, 12, 12 and 6 verses. Its opening, development and close span 6, 24 and 6.

edges.evidence: An English renku arrangement alternates discrete two- and three-line stanzas, including 2-line units. Traditional Japanese sound-unit groups need not be printed in this layout.
An English renku arrangement alternates discrete two- and three-line stanzas, including 3-line units. Traditional Japanese sound-unit groups need not be printed in this layout.

Rengay.note: The two-voice version totals 16 lines and the three-voice version 15. The source inventory gives 16 for both. A–C identify voices; all six verses develop one theme.

edges.evidence: Rengay uses haiku or haiku-like material. The recommendation does not make each verse a standalone haiku.
Rengay is a thematic alternative to renga or renku. Its six verses and single theme define a separate practice.
The two- and three-voice layouts include discrete 2-line linked verses.
The two- and three-voice layouts include discrete 3-line linked verses.

Haibun.note: One or more haiku link with prose. A haiku may close the piece or appear within it.

edges.evidence: The named verse component is one or more haiku.

Tanka prose.note: One or more tanka occur within or after prose. A contest may limit the count for its own entries.

edges.evidence: The row names tanka as the verse component interwoven with prose.

Sijo.note: The standard three-line form has two phrases per line and two segments per phrase. The 14–16 syllables per line are approximate; English typography may split these lines.

Tanaga.note: The catalog describes the traditional four seven-syllable lines on a single rhyme. The four marks apply to line endings.

edges.evidence: The traditional seven-syllable lines add a syllabic constraint to a four-line stanza on one rhyme.
The four-line stanza is a quatrain. The separate monorhymed-quatrain relationship adds its end-rhyme constraint.

Luc bat.note: In the standard chain the sixth positions rhyme; the eight-syllable line's ending supplies the rhyme carried into the next pair.

edges.evidence: The repeating metrical unit is a linked six-syllable and eight-syllable line pair.

Than-bauk.note: Each line has four syllables. Across the three lines the linked rhyme moves from syllable four to three to two.

edges.evidence: Each illustrated pattern specifies three lines in one stanza.

Cherita.note: A six-line story unfolds in stanzas of one, two and three lines. Their narrative roles are open.

edges.evidence: The second stanza comprises two lines.
The third stanza comprises three lines.

Englyn.note: Three variants illustrate a larger family. Milwr and penfyr have three lines; unodl union has four, with a short toddaid followed by a cywydd couplet.

edges.evidence: The unodl union variant ends with this specific seven-syllable couplet.
The milwr and penfyr variants shown are three-line stanzas.
The unodl union variant shown is a four-line stanza.
The unodl union variant contains a short toddaid and a two-line cywydd unit.

Cywydd deuair hirion.note: The unit has two rhyming seven-syllable lines with contrasting final accent. Neither order of stressed and unstressed endings is prescribed.

edges.evidence: Its recurring unit is a seven-syllable rhyming line pair with contrasting final accent.

Clogyrnach.note: The catalog prints six segments. The Welsh glossary groups them into two eight-syllable lines and one 16-syllable tail. The diagram shows the divisions within that tail.

edges.evidence: Two rhyming eight-syllable opening lines comprise one pair before the sixteen-syllable tail.

Gwawdodyn.note: Short and long versions open with two or four nine-syllable lines carrying the main rhyme. Their 10+9 closing couplet preserves that rhyme at the first-line break and final line end, with a second rhyme linking the tail to the interior of the final line.

edges.evidence: The short setting opens with a rhymed pair of nine-syllable lines. Both the short and long settings close with the metrically distinct two-line toddaid.
The six-line setting opens with a complete four-line monorhymed group before the two-line toddaid. The correspondence applies to this setting.

The hir branch and the pictured six-line setting both open with four monorhyming lines and close with a two-line toddaid. The opening lines have nine versus ten syllables, and the closing pair is 10–9 versus 10–10.

Hir a thoddaid.note: The common pattern has four ten-syllable opening lines and a 10+10 closing couplet. Its shared main rhyme and internal linking rhyme cross the couplet. Other opening lengths are documented. The inventory instead groups the first five lines together.

edges.evidence: A linked two-line toddaid closes the stanza, with a main rhyme and a second linking rhyme.
The common six-line stanza is a sestet. Documented four-, eight- and ten-line stanzas fall outside that correspondence.
The six-line setting opens with a complete four-line monorhymed group before the two-line toddaid. The correspondence applies to this setting.

Byr a thoddaid.note: The catalog gives an 8+8 unit with a 10+9 unit and four lines overall. The Welsh glossary describes four eight-syllable lines with a toddaid; the university dictionary specifies a short toddaid. The common components can be shown; exact count, length and order should stay open.

edges.evidence: Accounts disagree on the exact stanza length, yet both contain a closing or linked two-line toddaid unit.

Awdl gywydd.note: A seven-syllable couplet forms the unit. Its first end rhyme recurs within the second line. The example shows two units together; other lengths can repeat the unit.

edges.evidence: The catalog's four-line presentation groups two metrical couplets in a quatrain.
Each unit comprises two seven-syllable lines linked through end and internal rhyme.

Cyhydedd hir.note: The documented unit is nineteen syllables in four parts. The source shows two such groups; an invariant eight separate lines would misstate the unit.

Rhupunt.note: Welsh teaching examples distinguish 12-syllable short lines from 16-syllable long lines. Internal divisions and the shared line-ending rhyme are distinct.

Irish syllabic quatrains.note: The grouped measures differ. Deibhidhe and rannaigheacht mhór have seven-syllable lines; séadna alternates 8–7–8–7. In ae freislighe, end words alternate three and two syllables. The catalog treats dúnadh separately as poem-wide closure.

edges.evidence: The listed Irish measures use quatrains despite differences between their syllable counts.
The deibhidhe variant arranges the lines within its quatrain in rhyming pairs.

Pindaric ode.note: The antistrophe matches the preceding strophe's metrical design. The contrasting epode closes the triad; total triad count is open.

Limerick.note: The catalog's five-line template puts three beats in lines one, two and five, two in the others, and the same A rhyme on the punchline.

edges.evidence: The complete five-line stanza adds its own rhythm, word roles or line counts to the generic five-line unit.

Clerihew.note: A humorous biography takes the shape of a quatrain in two rhyming couplets. Line length can vary, and the first line usually ends in the subject’s name.

edges.evidence: AABB organizes the four lines into two rhyming couplets.
Its four lines form one stanza with an AABB scheme.

Double dactyl.note: Each of two quatrains has three double-dactyl lines and a shorter rhyming fourth line. A single-word double dactyl typically appears in the sixth line; the inventory compresses these distinctions.

edges.evidence: Each of two stanzas has four lines.

Ruthless rhyme.note: A deadpan AABB quatrain is one recorded shape. Other texts in this body of verse vary in length and rhyme.

edges.evidence: The displayed deadpan AABB template has four lines. The wider body of verse includes other lengths.
The displayed AABB version has two rhyming pairs. It is one template within a wider body of macabre verse.

Cinquain (Crapsey).note: The classic American accentual-syllabic stanza uses 2–4–6–8–2 syllables and typically 1–2–3–4–1 stresses. Iambic movement is usual; the earlier accentual pattern governs stresses alone.

edges.evidence: The complete five-line stanza adds its own rhythm, word roles or line counts to the generic five-line unit.

Didactic cinquain.note: The row defines line roles through a noun, adjectives, participles and a four-word phrase; the final synonym refers back to the opening noun.

edges.evidence: The complete five-line stanza adds its own rhythm, word roles or line counts to the generic five-line unit.

Diamante.note: The illustrated opposite-subject version organizes each line by word class. The four central nouns commonly divide between the two subjects; same-subject versions also occur.

edges.evidence: The specified seven-line arrangement is a seven-line unit with additional word rules.

Tetractys.note: The initial syllable counts rise one to four. The fifth line has ten syllables rather than continuing the arithmetic progression.

edges.evidence: The complete five-line stanza adds its own rhythm, word roles or line counts to the generic five-line unit.

Nonet.note: Nine syllabic lines descend from nine syllables to one. The row specifies no rhyme or multi-stanza division.

Etheree.note: The catalogued version increases from one syllable through ten, over ten lines, without rhyme requirements.

Fib.note: The catalog gives six Fibonacci counts. The diagram displays those six; it does not infer a fixed length for every extended Fibonacci poem.

edges.evidence: The six-line version shown is a six-line unit. Longer Fibonacci sequences fall beyond this comparison.

Lanterne.note: The final one-syllable line follows the four-syllable peak, matching the catalog's sharp taper.

edges.evidence: The complete five-line stanza adds its own rhythm, word roles or line counts to the generic five-line unit.

Shadorma.note: The source gives six consecutive syllabic counts, including identical third and fourth counts of three.

edges.evidence: The six-line stanza has fixed syllable counts.

Hay(na)ku.note: The source explicitly permits two directions. Each alternative counts words across three lines, with six words in either version.

edges.evidence: Each illustrated pattern specifies three lines in one stanza.

Lune.note: One three-line variant counts syllables 5–3–5. Another counts words 3–5–3.

edges.evidence: Each illustrated pattern specifies three lines in one stanza.

American sentence.note: The catalog gives one line containing 17 syllables. This is also a specific one-line construction; no additional lines may be inferred.

edges.evidence: A seventeen-syllable, one-line poem meets the catalog's definition of a monostich.

Monostich.note: One line constitutes the whole poem in this row. The related American sentence is a particular one-line form rather than a metrical requirement.

edges.evidence: American sentence is an example of a form that is always a monostich in this catalog.

Sevenling.note: The source specifies two tercets, each featuring three items, and a twist in the single closing line. It does not distribute items one per line.

edges.evidence: The two opening stanzas are explicitly tercets.

Kwansaba.note: The usual design has seven lines and seven words per line. Proper nouns, foreign terms and quoted passages may exceed the seven-letter limit that the catalog states without exceptions.

edges.evidence: The specified seven-line arrangement is a seven-line unit with additional word rules.

Zeno.note: The first eight-syllable line precedes three 4–2–1 groups. All three closing one-syllable lines rhyme.

Abecedarian.note: The initial letters proceed alphabetically. The source allows the organizing unit to be a stanza, so 26 letter positions do not guarantee 26 printed lines.

Golden shovel.note: The borrowed line's successive words control successive new line endings. Its length in words controls the new line count. Displaying an epigraph is not inferred as mandatory.

Bop.note: In the common three-stanza arrangement, six, eight and six lines develop the argument. A refrain follows each stanza. The last can show an attempted resolution that fails; some variants continue to a fourth stanza.

edges.evidence: The first and third argumentative stanzas each consist of six lines before the refrain.
The middle stanza of the common version consists of eight lines; it illustrates the generic octave, without the specialized huitain meter or scheme.

Paradelle.note: The poem has four six-line stanzas. In each of the first three, repeat two lines in pairs and recombine all and only their words across the closing two lines. The final stanza recombines the preceding stanzas’ vocabulary.

edges.evidence: All four stanzas consist of six lines.
The last two lines of each of the first three stanzas form a pair governed by the recombination rule.
In each of the first three six-line stanzas, the four opening positions contain two doubled lines. They constitute the designated opening group before the recombining couplet.
